intro: Every ride on a skateboard is a science lesson on wheels. A foot pushes the ground, and the board starts to roll. A pebble stops a wheel, and the rider keeps going. A skater drops down a ramp, speeds up, then slows as she climbs the other side. Each of these moments has a cause you can name.

In this unit you will meet the forces that move a board: pushes, pulls, friction and gravity. You will learn about inertia and Isaac Newton's first law. Then you will follow energy as it trades from height to speed and back on a ramp, and see where some of it goes.

By the end, you will be able to explain why a board slows down, why soft wheels roll over cracks, and why a higher start means more speed. You will also know how to use a foot brake, how to fall small, and how skaters pump to keep going on a halfpipe.
bigQuestion: What forces and energy changes make a skateboard start, speed up, slow down and stop?

test.why: A force is a push or a pull, and every force has a size and a direction.

test.q: Your back foot pushes backward on the ground. Which way does the board go?
test.why: Your foot pushes back on the ground and the ground pushes you forward in return.

choices: A board resting on flat ground
A skater's push starting a board rolling
A board sitting in a garage
test.why: An unbalanced force changes motion. A push that starts a board rolling is unbalanced.

test.q: A wheel hits a pebble and the board stops. What carries the rider forward?
test.why: Nothing stops the rider's body, so inertia keeps it moving forward.

test.q: What should you avoid when you fall?
choices: Catching yourself with locked, straight arms
test.why: Locked arms can hurt your wrists. Get low, tuck and roll instead.

test.q: On which surface does a board roll farthest after one push?
test.why: A smooth floor makes the least friction, so the board rolls farthest.

test.q: In a foot brake, what does the back foot do?
choices: Brushes the ground lightly, then presses
test.why: The back foot brushes the ground, then presses gently to make friction and slow down.

test.q: What did Newton's first law describe?
choices: Inertia: objects keep their motion unless a force changes it
test.why: Newton's first law, from the Principia of 1687, describes inertia.

test.q: Why did urethane wheels help skaters?
choices: They gripped and rolled over cracks and pebbles
test.why: Soft urethane wheels squish around bumps and grip the ground, so cracks stop them less.
On the durometer A scale, a lower number means a softer wheel.

test.q: A skater stands still on top of a tall ramp. What does she have?
test.why: Height gives her stored, or potential, energy. She is still, so she has no kinetic energy yet.

test.q: As a skater rolls up a ramp wall, what happens?
choices: Her stored energy becomes motion energy
Her motion energy turns into stored energy
test.why: Climbing, she slows down as motion energy turns back into stored energy.

test.q: Who goes faster at the bottom, rolling without pushing?
test.why: A higher start stores more energy, which becomes more speed at the bottom.

test.q: Why can a rolling skater who adds no energy never climb higher than her start?
choices: Friction turns some energy into heat and sound
test.why: Friction takes a share of energy each trip, and energy cannot be made from nothing.

test.q: How does a skater pump on a halfpipe?
choices: Drags a foot on the flat bottom
Crouches into the curve and stands tall as it lifts her
test.why: Crouching into the curve and standing tall as it lifts her lets her legs add energy.

write.prompt: A skater rolls from the deck of a small ramp, down the transition, across the flat bottom and up the other wall. Explain what happens to her energy at each spot, why she cannot climb higher than her start without pumping, and how friction and pumping change the story.
tips: Name the energy at each spot: stored energy, motion energy, or both.
Say where she is fastest and why.
Explain where friction sends some energy: heat and sound.
Describe pumping step by step: crouch into the curve, stand tall as it lifts you.
Use at least four words from the unit, such as potential energy, kinetic energy, friction and transition.
